data.title: Initialize go spike contract
data.context: Reusable repo-local agent workflow stack. Make go/go-auto/go-loop practical: route rough Viggo commands, create or repair repo-local .go state, execute autonomously inside safety gates, validate with tests, and document exact operator usage.
data.decision: Use repo-local .go vision, principles, epics, tasks, evidence, and go auto loop for this project.
consequences: go auto can continue from repo state

data.title: Make go-auto executable through a run envelope
data.context: go auto must be control handoff, not only task-list output; Hermes needs machine-readable preflight, budget, stop, checkpoint, and result boundaries.
data.decision: go auto emits execution_policy and run_envelope; repo-local go-workflow-stack now owns its own .go vision, principles, tasks, evidence, and decisions.
consequences: Hermes can execute go auto with less chat inference
Future executor work can target the auto-run-result schema

data.title: Make go auto a command train, not a command suggestion
data.context: Viggo reports go auto is not autonomous enough: he still has to spam obvious follow-up commands that should be chained by the workflow.
data.decision: go auto must mean agent control handoff: inspect route/status, claim or create the next task, execute verification/build/recheck/finish loops, create same-scope follow-ups, and continue until done, blocker, or explicit budget. The stack should emit/enforce a command-train contract, and Hermes skills should execute it with tools rather than returning instructions for Viggo to run.
consequences: Future stack work prioritizes autonomous train execution, budgets, continuation checkpoints, and fewer user-triggered micro-commands.

data.title: Use a compact execution brief as the advice handoff
data.context: Long recommendations are useful for reasoning but unreliable as an execution contract and force repeated prompts.
data.decision: Persist a schema-validated compact execution brief containing the problem, chosen approach, bounded work units, acceptance, verification, non-goals, and recommendation provenance.
consequences: The Go command can create semantically scoped tasks from the brief and, when execution is authorized, immediately run them.

data.title: Versioned stakeholder delivery contract
data.context: Substantial .go assignments need a consistent output that non-technical stakeholders can understand without repository or GitHub access.
data.decision: Define go-workflow.delivery.v1 with mandatory summary, assignment, delivered scope, excluded scope, evidence summary, limitations, open points, next steps, release identity, disclosure class, and machine-readable provenance. Stakeholder narrative is rendered in HTML while provenance remains structured and independently hashable.
consequences: Every generated delivery is comparable and forwardable; HTML remains derived output and never replaces repo-local JSON or JSONL state.

data.title: Portable first and publication adapter second
data.context: Stakeholders may lack GitHub access and projects may not exist on GitHub while public hosting can create privacy and revocation risks.
data.decision: The mandatory output is a self-contained HTML file plus JSON manifest. Building is local and side-effect free. Publishing is a separate explicit command through adapters. Initial stack scope implements file output only and defines a publisher interface; link-public or controlled hosting is an opt-in extension.
consequences: Every project can deliver without external infrastructure; hosting credentials and public side effects cannot block report generation or happen implicitly.

data.title: Fail-closed delivery disclosure classes
data.context: Generated stakeholder reports can accidentally expose local paths, prompts, credentials, customer data, internal logs, or repository-only evidence.
data.decision: Every delivery declares public, link-private, or restricted. The generator scans all rendered and manifest text for secret-like keys, credential files, local home paths, raw prompts, and unapproved customer identifiers. Unknown or omitted disclosure defaults to restricted. Publication requires explicit disclosure and a clean scan.
consequences: Generation remains useful for private delivery while public publication fails closed instead of assuming repository evidence is safe to disclose.

data.title: Immutable assignment delivery releases
data.context: A large assignment needs a stable handoff while corrections and later work must remain auditable rather than silently replacing what was sent.
data.decision: Deliveries are created explicitly for an epic or selected task set. States are draft, released, and superseded. Release ids combine a semantic slug and monotonically increasing version. Released artifacts are immutable; corrections create a new version that may supersede an earlier release.
consequences: Recipients can refer to an exact delivery and later corrections preserve the historical record. Individual task completion alone does not automatically publish a report.

data.title: Editorial evidence-led stakeholder delivery
data.context: The generated report must be readable, printable, mobile-safe, and directly forwardable without looking like a generic SaaS dashboard or internal agent transcript.
data.decision: Use an editorial report composition with strong release identity, readable typography, restrained green accent, explicit delivered versus excluded scope, evidence rows, limitations, and disclosure notice. Avoid card stacking and repository-centric jargon in the visible narrative.
consequences: The renderer has a concrete visual contract and can be regression-tested against named sections and responsive overflow.
